title: Reverse Linked List
description: Walk the list once; at each node rewrite next to point at the previous node. Three pointers: prev, curr, next.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given the head of a singly linked list and I need to reverse it in place, returning the new head. So [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [5,4,3,2,1] — same nodes, same values, but the next pointers all flip."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Mutation — am I allowed to rewrite the existing `next` pointers, or do I need to allocate new nodes?
• Empty list — head is null. Return null?
• Single node — return the same node (its next is already null)?
• Iterative or recursive — any preference? (Iterative is O(1) space; recursive is O(n) stack.)
sections.why: The mutation question is the load-bearing one. If they want immutability, this becomes a different problem — you'd allocate a new list, which is O(n) extra space. If they're fine with in-place mutation (the standard answer), the iterative three-pointer dance is O(1) space. The empty/single-node questions surface that your loop should handle them without special cases — and they will, if you set `prev = null` at the start.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n) extra-space solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is: walk the list and push every value into an array, then walk a second time and overwrite each node's `val` from the array in reverse — or build a brand new list from `arr.reverse()`. Either way it's O(n) time and O(n) extra space. Functionally correct, but if I'm allowed to mutate next pointers I can do it in one pass with O(1) extra space — same comparisons, just rewriting the existing pointers instead of allocating an array."
sections.why: Two reasons to name the array-buffer brute force out loud. (1) It proves you can see the obvious answer before reaching for the clever one — interviewers worry about candidates who pattern-match straight to the three-pointer dance without acknowledging why it's better. (2) It frames the iterative solution as 'same outcome, just no buffer' rather than a wholly different algorithm — which is what makes the pointer dance feel motivated rather than magical.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to the three-pointer dance?
sections.say: "Reversing a singly linked list is the canonical 'pointer-dance' problem — you can't walk backward (no prev pointer in the node), so you have to flip each `next` as you pass through, but the moment you flip `curr.next = prev` you've lost the rest of the list. The fix is to cache `next` BEFORE the rewrite. That gives you the three-pointer template: `prev` (what comes before, starts null), `curr` (where I am now), and a local `next` cached each iteration. Initialize `prev = null` because the original head becomes the new tail with `next = null`. Return `prev` at the end, not `curr` — when the loop exits, `curr` is null and `prev` points to what was the old tail."
sections.why: Naming the pattern *and* the structural reason makes it land. 'Three-pointer dance' alone is jargon; 'three pointers because flipping curr.next destroys the forward link, so you must cache next first' is a derivation. Interviewers grade on the second. Calling out 'return prev, not curr' upfront also short-circuits the most common off-by-one — most candidates write the loop right and then return the wrong thing.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a typical multi-node reversal, the empty case where the loop never runs, and the single-node case where the loop runs exactly once.

examples.note: Classic case — five iterations of the pointer dance, prev walks from null to 5.
examples.trace:
init: prev=null, curr=1
iter1: next=2, 1.next=null, prev=1, curr=2  → reversedSoFar=[1]
iter2: next=3, 2.next=1, prev=2, curr=3     → reversedSoFar=[2,1]
iter3: next=4, 3.next=2, prev=3, curr=4     → reversedSoFar=[3,2,1]
iter4: next=5, 4.next=3, prev=4, curr=5     → reversedSoFar=[4,3,2,1]
iter5: next=null, 5.next=4, prev=5, curr=null → reversedSoFar=[5,4,3,2,1]
loop exits (curr=null), return prev=5

examples.note: Empty list — head is null, loop never executes, prev stays null, return null. No special case needed.
examples.trace:
init: prev=null, curr=null
loop check: curr is null → never enter
return prev=null

examples.note: Single node — one iteration writes 42.next=null (it already was), then curr becomes null. Same code, no special case.
examples.trace:
init: prev=null, curr=42
iter1: next=null, 42.next=null, prev=42, curr=null
loop exits, return prev=42

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the two off-by-ones this problem rewards. (1) The empty-list trace confirms that initializing `prev = null` and looping on `curr` (not `head`) handles the zero-node case without an `if`. (2) The single-node trace confirms you return `prev`, not `curr` — at loop exit `curr` is always null, so returning `curr` would always give you back null. Writing the trace out before the code is much less painful than catching either bug after the interviewer points at failing tests.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty list (head = null) → loop never runs, prev stays null, return null. ✓
• Single node → one iteration sets the (already null) next, then curr becomes null, return that node. ✓
• Two nodes → tests the rewrite specifically — 1→2 becomes 2→1, easy to mess up if you forget to cache next.
• Long list (10k+ nodes) → O(n) time, O(1) space; the recursive version would blow the stack here, which is one reason to prefer iterative.
• Cycle in the input (e.g. 1→2→3→1) → the loop never terminates. Worth flagging that this function assumes acyclic input; with a cycle you'd need Floyd's detection first."
sections.why: The empty and single-node cases both work for the *same* structural reason — `prev = null` is the correct initial value and the loop condition checks `curr`, not `head` — and naming that connection shows you understand the invariant rather than memorizing pass/fail per case. The cycle call-out is the senior move; most candidates assume acyclic input silently, and the interviewer either nods (impressed) or says 'good catch but assume acyclic for now'. Either outcome is good.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — each node is visited exactly once. The body of the loop is a fixed number of pointer assignments (three), so no amortization argument is needed.

Space is O(1) — three local pointers (`prev`, `curr`, `next`) regardless of list length. The recursive version is O(n) stack space because every call frame holds onto a node, so for large lists iterative is the right call.

If you wanted to extend to 'reverse only nodes between positions m and n', it's the same three-pointer dance bounded by a counter — walk to position m-1, then run the reverse loop n-m+1 times, then splice the reversed segment back in. Same template, just bracketed. And if you wanted to 'reverse in groups of k' (LeetCode 25), it's the same dance run k nodes at a time with a per-group splice."
sections.why: The fixed-work-per-node argument is the clean defense — there's no nested loop here so amortization isn't the issue, but interviewers do sometimes ask 'why isn't this O(n²)?' and the answer is just 'every operation in the body is O(1)'. The 'reverse between m and n' and 'reverse k-group' extensions prove you see the three-pointer dance as a reusable primitive rather than this one problem's trick — that's exactly how it shows up in Reverse Nodes in k-Group, Reverse Linked List II, and as a subroutine inside Reorder List and Palindrome Linked List.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the canonical three-pointer reversal one statement at a time. The highlighted line is what just ran; the state panel shows prev/curr/next and the list rebuilt as an array after each step.
trace: function* trace(input) {
const toArr = (n) => { const out = []; while (n) { out.push(n.val); n = n.next; } return out; };
const dummy = { val: null, next: null };
let tail = dummy;
for (const v of input) { tail.next = { val: v, next: null }; tail = tail.next; }
let head = dummy.next;
yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — list ${JSON.stringify(input)}`, state: { input, list: toArr(head) } };
let prev = null, curr = head;
yield { line: 3, label: 'init prev=null, curr=head', state: { list: toArr(head), prev: null, curr: curr ? curr.val : null } };
while (curr) {
yield { line: 4, label: `loop entry — curr=${curr.val}`, state: { remaining: toArr(curr), reversedSoFar: toArr(prev), prev: prev ? prev.val : null, curr: curr.val } };
const next = curr.next;

yield { line: 6, label: `cache next = ${next ? next.val : 'null'} (saved before rewrite)`, state: { remaining: toArr(curr), reversedSoFar: toArr(prev), prev: prev ? prev.val : null, curr: curr.val, next: next ? next.val : null } };
curr.next = prev;

yield { line: 7, label: `rewrite curr.next → prev (${curr.val}.next = ${prev ? prev.val : 'null'})`, state: { reversedSoFar: toArr(curr), prev: prev ? prev.val : null, curr: curr.val, next: next ? next.val : null } };
prev = curr;
yield { line: 8, label: `prev → ${prev.val}`, state: { reversedSoFar: toArr(prev), prev: prev.val, curr: curr.val, next: next ? next.val : null } };
curr = next;
yield { line: 9, label: `curr → ${curr ? curr.val : 'null'} (advance using cached next)`, state: { reversedSoFar: toArr(prev), prev: prev.val, curr: curr ? curr.val : null } };
yield { line: 12, label: `loop done — return prev (new head)`, state: { reversed: toArr(prev), prev: prev ? prev.val : null, curr: null, returns: JSON.stringify(toArr(prev)) } };

notes: Cache curr.next BEFORE rewriting curr.next = prev, otherwise you lose the rest of the list.
Return prev, not curr — curr is null at the end; prev is the new head.
Start prev = null so the original head becomes the new tail with next = null.
reference.crux: Walk once with three pointers (prev/curr/next); cache curr.next BEFORE flipping curr.next = prev, so the rewrite can't strand the rest of the list.
cruxDistractors: Push every value into an array, then overwrite each node's val from the array read back-to-front.
Recurse to the tail, then on the unwind set head.next.next = head — clean, but O(n) call-stack space.
Keep two pointers (prev, curr) and swap with a destructuring assignment, no cached next needed.

alternates.label: Recursive (unwind from tail)
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer wants to see the recursive formulation or you're warming up for problems like Reverse Nodes in k-Group where a recursive subroutine slots in naturally. Skip it on production-sized inputs — JS has no TCO, so n deep recursion blows the stack around ~10k nodes.
notes: Recurse all the way to the tail FIRST; the tail bubbles up as newHead unchanged through every return.
On unwind, `head.next.next = head` flips the link backward, then `head.next = null` severs the forward pointer so the new tail terminates cleanly.
Space is O(n) for the call stack — one frame per node. For long lists prefer the iterative version; JS doesn't optimize tail calls here anyway (the recursion isn't in tail position).

questions.q: Why cache curr.next before reassigning curr.next?
options: JS evaluates right-to-left, so `curr.next = prev` reads curr.next first anyway — the cache is just defensive
Otherwise you lose the rest of the list
Without caching, `prev` would hold a stale pointer to the old head
Reassigning a `.next` property is illegal without first reading it on some JS engines

questions.explain: When the loop exits, curr is null and prev points to the new head.

options: So `prev = curr` on iter 1 makes the original head point at itself, terminating the list
So the original head ends up with next = null (new tail)
Because `null` is the only falsy value the `while (curr)` loop accepts as a starting state
It signals the GC that the original list can be freed once curr advances past it

questions.q: Space complexity of the iterative version?
Why is the recursive reversal O(n) space while the iterative version is O(1)?
options: Recursion copies the whole list at each call
Each recursive call holds a stack frame, so n nodes means n frames on the call stack
Recursion allocates a new node per call
There is no space difference — both are O(1)
questions.explain: Recursion uses O(n) call-stack frames (one per node); the iterative loop reuses three local pointers regardless of length.

questions.q: On a 1-million-node list, why might the recursive version crash while the iterative one is fine?
options: JS has no tail-call optimization, so n deep recursion overflows the call stack
The iterative version is faster so it finishes first
Recursion produces the wrong answer on long lists
questions.explain: Engines don't apply TCO here, so ~1M nested frames blow the stack; the iterative loop has constant stack depth.

questions.q: If you write `prev = curr; curr.next = prev;` (reorder the two assignments), what breaks?
options: curr.next = prev now points the node at itself, creating a self-loop
It reverses twice and returns the original list
questions.explain: Setting prev = curr first makes prev === curr, so curr.next = prev points the node back to itself instead of the previous node.

questions.q: What is the value of `curr` when the while loop exits?
questions.explain: The loop condition is `while (curr)`, so it exits exactly when curr becomes null — which is why you return prev, not curr.

questions.q: For a two-node list [1,2], what does node 1's `next` point to after reversal?
questions.explain: The original head (1) becomes the new tail, so its next is null — that comes from prev starting as null.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the iterative 3-pointer reversal. Blanks isolate the dance, not the field name.

blanks.hint: what is before the original head?
flip curr.next backward — the central rewrite
advance prev — what was current becomes the new previous
advance curr using the value cached one line above
the new head when curr is null
